solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

flags: minor: key closely paraphrases the paragraph 5 claim that the fly hypothesis has what its rivals lack, so the item is close to a lookup
minor: A (camouflage) is the main trap for readers who stop after paragraph 2; B and C are weak and few will pick them
R035-01.notes: Passage moves from many explanations, to camouflage being undercut (2016), to fly correlation (2014) and experiments (2019), and concludes the fly idea has unique experimental support. D. C contradicts 'rivals have so far lacked'; B is unsupported.

R035-02.notes: The sentence sets up the rest of the passage: tests that can discriminate among hypotheses. B overstates (not 'disproved'); C invents lost interest; D is wrong because the fly idea is not introduced there.

flags: minor: A is a plausible trap for students who read 'took seriously' as 'agreed with'
R035-03.notes: The study treated the claim about predator vision as worth testing and modeled visual acuity. It did not agree (A), the authors used animal vision rather than human vision (C), and they did not measure hearing or smell (D).

flags: minor: D (zebras detect lions first) may tempt some students, though the passage says nothing about the zebras' detection
R035-04.notes: Within the range where the stripes are visible, the lion has already detected the prey by other senses, so the stripes add no hiding value even there. A overgeneralizes ('every'); B is invented.

flags: minor: key echoes paragraph 5 ('experiments in which the pattern was the only thing that changed'), which makes it near-lookup; C and D are off-topic, so effectively a 2-choice item (A vs B)
R035-05.notes: The 2014 analysis was correlational; the 2019 study manipulated the coat pattern and found that fly behavior changed. Rated at the low edge of medium (two steps across paragraphs 3-4).

flags: minor: the key restates the next sentence in the passage (fewer landings), so locating it is quick; partly overlaps with R035-09 choice C, which also turns on circling frequency, though it doesn't reveal that item's answer
R035-06.notes: Equal circling means flies find zebras just as well; the difference shows up only in landings. A contradicts that; B is unsupported; C ignores the landing difference.

flags: minor: shares the coat experiment with R035-05, but neither item gives away the other's answer
R035-07.notes: The uncovered heads act as a control: same horse, same flies, no change in landings on the head, so the coat's pattern caused the reduction on the body. C is contradicted (the head is not protected); B and D are unsupported. Students must recognize the control logic, which is the hard step.

flags: minor: A ('winners') is the usual common-meaning trap; B and D are seldom chosen
R035-08.notes: 'Each idea has had its champions' means advocates or supporters.

R035-09.notes: The fly hypothesis rests partly on the 2014 finding that striping tracks where flies are active; boldest stripes where flies are rare would cut against it. A bears on camouflage, not flies; B fits the passage's 'more than one purpose' point and does not weaken it; C is a trap, but circling was never the effect that mattered (landing was), so a slight circling difference does not undermine the hypothesis.
